To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the conservation of woodland in England has been achieved through statutory protection of sites, through statutory policies on forestry, and through incentives to landowners and managers to protect and enhance wildlife on private lands; 2) the statutory protected sites have been increased in size through successive legislation in the last half century; 3) the statutory policies on forestry have been strengthened over the last 25 years to promote the conservation of wildlife on private lands.

the English experience has shown the importance of the following: (1) a long-term commitment to woodland nature conservation; (2) a wide range of approaches, including statutory and voluntary, and (3) a willingness of landowners to engage with conservationists.

(1) woodland on private land in England is protected through a combination of statutory nature conservation designations, forestry legislation and incentives for voluntary nature conservation; (2) the degree of protection afforded varies between sites, but the overall area of woodland protected is much greater than that afforded by statutory nature reserves alone; and (3) these approaches may be relevant to other countries where woodland is part of a cultural or historical landscape.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the conservation of wildlife in private woodland.
the conservation and management of woodland in privately-owned cultural landscape.
the development of approaches in England to protect and conserve woodland on private lands.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the English experience of woodland conservation has been a success.
the English approach has worked well.

the English experience has demonstrated that the protection of woodland in a cultural landscape, and in particular the protection of woodland for nature conservation, is possible on a large scale, through a combination of statutory protection and voluntary measures, and that this is a more cost-effective approach than nature reserves alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have been able to demonstrate that the English experience has been a successful approach to the protection of woodland in cultural landscapes and that the lessons learnt in England may be relevant in the context of the wider European experience.
we have achieved a good level of protection for woodland on private lands through a combination of statutory and voluntary measures.

the conservation of woodland and wildlife in England has been successful because: (1) a wide range of policies has been developed, each with its own strengths; (2) the policies are flexible and adaptable, and can respond quickly to changing priorities; (3) the policies work at different scales and are applied to different types of woodland; and (4) there has been a strong commitment to woodland and wildlife conservation by government, landowners and other stakeholders.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the English experience shows that it is possible to conserve woodland in a cultural landscape, even if that landscape has been modified by human activities.
there is a need to consider the role of the private sector in conservation, and that the role of the government in promoting voluntary conservation is an important factor in this.
it is possible to achieve conservation of woodland on privately owned lands through a variety of means, including statutory protection and incentives.
